# University of Chicago Summary
The University of Chicago, founded in 1890 with significant support from John D. Rockefeller and local donors, grew rapidly under its first president, William Rainey Harper. It pioneered the quarter system, Socratic teaching methods, the Core Curriculum, and the Great Books program in undergraduate education. The university faced financial challenges and rebounded with strategic fundraising and endowment growth, evolving through significant presidents such as Robert Maynard Hutchins and Hanna Holborn Gray. Major milestones include its decisive role in the Manhattan Project, the emergence of the influential Chicago schools of economics and sociology, and continuous expansion into interdisciplinary research, professional education, and global campuses.
Located on 217 acres in Hyde Park, Chicago, the university is known for its Collegiate Gothic architecture and historic sites, including the location of the first nuclear chain reaction. Its academic structure comprises the undergraduate College, four graduate divisions, and seven professional schools, enabling rigorous research across diverse fields. The University of Chicago consistently ranks among the world’s top universities in global and national rankings and boasts a library system with over 11 million volumes. With an enrollment of approximately 7,569 undergraduates and 10,968 graduates in 2024, the university maintains a highly selective admissions process and a vibrant campus life, supporting over 400 student organizations. Chicago alumni and faculty include 101 Nobel laureates, numerous government leaders, and pioneers in science, law, business, and the arts.
